metadata.title: Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks as Generative Models

extraction_notes.note: The experimental evidence is in tables (NLL per data set) and figures; the tables and figure captions are not nodes, and the claims read off them carry rigor numerical.

Data-set descriptions and hyperparameter choices in Sections 5.1-5.2 (one-hot d=96 encoding, sequence lengths, hidden sizes, learning-rate grid, music data details) and future-work sentences without mathematical content were left as text.
Baselines and evaluation protocols described in prose were typed as algorithms; AP4 (one-way inference) is a single operation and gets zero steps.

The Bayesian MCMC description spans the Bayes'-theorem derivation; the derivation sentence with Eq. (8) is a nested claim and the algorithm steps are the Gibbs-sampling and proposal-enumeration sentences around it.

nodes.name: Recurrent neural network
nodes.statement: Recurrent neural networks \citep{rumelhart1986learning,haykin2009neural} can be seen as extensions of the standard feedforward multilayer perceptron networks, where the inputs and outputs are sequences instead of individual observations.
nodes.genus: extensions of the standard feedforward multilayer perceptron networks
differentia: the inputs and outputs are sequences instead of individual observations

nodes.name: Input sequence X
nodes.statement: Let us denote the input to a recurrent neural network by $\mathbf{X} = \left\lbrace \mathbf{x}_t \right\rbrace$ where $\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^N$ is an input vector for each time step $t$.

nodes.name: Output sequence Y
nodes.statement: Let us further denote the output as $\mathbf{Y} = \left\lbrace \mathbf{y}_t \right\rbrace$ where $\mathbf{y}_t \in \mathbb{R}^M$ is an output vector for each time step $t$.

nodes.name: Unsupervised RNN by next-input prediction
nodes.statement: Although RNNs map input sequences to output sequences, we can use them in an unsupervised manner by letting the RNN predict the next input. We can do so by setting $\mathbf{Y} = \left\lbrace \mathbf{y}_t = \mathbf{x}_{t+1} \right\rbrace$.
nodes.statement_short: An RNN is used unsupervised by predicting the next input, $\mathbf{y}_t=\mathbf{x}_{t+1}$.

nodes.name: Unidirectional recurrent neural network
nodes.statement: The structure of a basic RNN with one hidden layer is illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:rnn_architecture}, where the output $\mathbf{y}_t$ is determined by \begin{equation} P\left(\mathbf{y}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^t\right) = \mathrm{\phi} \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y} \mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{y} \right) \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \mathbf{h}_t = \tanh \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{h} \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{x} \mathbf{x}_{t} + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{h} \right) \end{equation} and $\mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y}$, $\mathbf{W}_\mathrm{h}$, and $\mathbf{W}_\mathrm{x}$ are the weight matrices connecting the hidden to output layer, hidden to hidden layer, and input to hidden layer, respectively.
nodes.definiendum: basic RNN with one hidden layer
nodes.statement_short: One-hidden-layer RNN: output $\phi(W_y h_t + b_y)$ with tanh recurrence $h_t$ on $h_{t-1}$ and $x_t$.

nodes.name: Unidirectional RNN output distribution
nodes.statement: P\left(\mathbf{y}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^t\right) = \mathrm{\phi} \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y} \mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{y} \right)
nodes.label: eq:uni_y

nodes.name: Unidirectional RNN hidden state recurrence
nodes.statement: \mathbf{h}_t = \tanh \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{h} \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{x} \mathbf{x}_{t} + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{h} \right)
nodes.label: eq:uni_h

nodes.name: Bias vectors b_y, b_h
nodes.statement: $\mathbf{b}_\mathrm{y}$ and $\mathbf{b}_\mathrm{h}$ are the output and hidden layer bias vectors, respectively.

nodes.name: Final nonlinearity phi
nodes.statement: Typical options for the final nonlinearity $\mathrm{\phi}$ are the softmax function for classification or categorical prediction tasks, or independent Bernoulli variables with sigmoid functions for other binary prediction tasks.
nodes.statement_short: The output nonlinearity $\phi$ is a softmax for categorical tasks or independent sigmoid Bernoullis for binary tasks.

nodes.name: RNN output depends only on the past
nodes.statement: In this form, the RNN therefore evaluates the output $\mathbf{y}_t$ based on information propagated through the hidden layer that directly or indirectly depends on the observations $\{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^t= \{\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_t\}$.

nodes.name: Bidirectional recurrent neural network (BRNN)
nodes.statement: Bidirectional RNNs (BRNN) \citep{schuster1997bidirectional,baldi1999exploiting} extend the unidirectional RNN by introducing a second hidden layer, where the hidden to hidden connections flow in opposite temporal order.
differentia: introducing a second hidden layer, where the hidden to hidden connections flow in opposite temporal order

nodes.name: Proposed BRNN output formulation
nodes.statement: The output $\mathbf{y}_t$ is traditionally determined by \begin{equation*} P\left(\mathbf{y}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t}\right) = \mathrm{\phi} \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y}^\mathrm{f} \mathbf{h}_{t}^\mathrm{f} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y}^\mathrm{b} \mathbf{h}_{t}^\mathrm{b} + \mathbf{b}_y \right), \end{equation*} but we propose the use of \begin{equation} P\left(\mathbf{y}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t}\right) = \mathrm{\phi} \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y}^\mathrm{f} \mathbf{h}_{t-1}^\mathrm{f} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y}^\mathrm{b} \mathbf{h}_{t+1}^\mathrm{b} + \mathbf{b}_y \right) \end{equation} where \begin{align} \mathbf{h}_t^\mathrm{f} &= \tanh \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{f} \mathbf{h}^\mathrm{f} _{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{x}^\mathrm{f} \mathbf{x}_{t} + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{f} \right) \\ \mathbf{h}_t^\mathrm{b} &= \tanh \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{b} \mathbf{h}^\mathrm{b}_{t+1} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{x}^\mathrm{b} \mathbf{x}_{t} + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{b} \right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Instead of $h_t^f,h_t^b$, the output at $t$ is computed from $h_{t-1}^f$ and $h_{t+1}^b$, so it excludes $x_t$.

nodes.name: Proposed BRNN output distribution
nodes.statement: P\left(\mathbf{y}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t}\right) = \mathrm{\phi} \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y}^\mathrm{f} \mathbf{h}_{t-1}^\mathrm{f} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y}^\mathrm{b} \mathbf{h}_{t+1}^\mathrm{b} + \mathbf{b}_y \right)
nodes.label: eq:bi_y

nodes.name: BRNN forward and backward hidden recurrences
nodes.statement: \mathbf{h}_t^\mathrm{f} &= \tanh \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{f} \mathbf{h}^\mathrm{f} _{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{x}^\mathrm{f} \mathbf{x}_{t} + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{f} \right) \\ \mathbf{h}_t^\mathrm{b} &= \tanh \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{b} \mathbf{h}^\mathrm{b}_{t+1} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{x}^\mathrm{b} \mathbf{x}_{t} + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{b} \right).
nodes.label: eq:bi_hf

nodes.name: Forward/backward superscripts f and b
nodes.statement: Compared with the regular RNN, the forward and backward directions have separate non-tied weights and hidden activations, and are denoted by the superscript f and b for forward and backward, respectively.

nodes.name: Proposed BRNN output excludes x_t
nodes.statement: Note also that in the proposed formulation, $\mathbf{y}_{t}$ does not get information from $\mathbf{x}_{t}$.

nodes.name: Unsupervised BRNN by setting Y = X
nodes.statement: We can therefore use the model in an unsupervised manner to predict one time step given all other time steps in the input sequence simply by setting $\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}$.

nodes.name: Unidirectional joint factorization
nodes.statement: Probabilistic unsupervised modeling for sequences using a unidirectional RNN is straightforward, as the joint distribution for the whole sequence is simply the product of the individual predictions: \begin{align} P_{\mathrm{unidirectional}}(\mathbf{X}) = \prod_{t=1}^T P(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1}). \end{align}
conclusions: the joint distribution for the whole sequence is simply the product of the individual predictions
nodes.statement_short: With a unidirectional RNN the sequence likelihood is the product of the one-step predictions.

nodes.name: Unidirectional joint distribution
nodes.statement: P_{\mathrm{unidirectional}}(\mathbf{X}) = \prod_{t=1}^T P(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1}).

nodes.name: BRNN joint distribution is not a product of its conditionals
nodes.statement: For the BRNN, the situation is more complicated. The network gives predictions for individual outputs given all the others, and the joint distribution cannot be written as their product. We propose two solutions for this, denoted by \emph{GSN} and \emph{NADE}.

nodes.name: Generative Stochastic Network (GSN)
nodes.statement: {\bf GSN} Generative Stochastic Networks (GSN) \citep{bengio2013generalized} use a denoising auto-encoder to estimate the data distribution as the asymptotic distribution of the Markov chain that alternates between corruption and denoising. The resulting distribution is thus defined only implicitly, and cannot be written analytically.
nodes.statement_short: A GSN defines the data distribution implicitly as the stationary law of a corrupt-then-denoise Markov chain.

nodes.name: Masking corruption and BRNN denoising function
nodes.statement: We can define a corruption function that masks $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ as missing, and a denoising function that reconstructs it from the others.

nodes.name: One BRNN feedforward pass is the denoising function
nodes.statement: It turns out that one feedforward pass of the BRNN does exactly that.
conclusions: one feedforward pass of the BRNN does exactly that

nodes.name: GSN interpretation of the BRNN
nodes.statement: Our first probabilistic interpretation is thus that the joint distribution defined by a BRNN is the asymptotic distribution of a process that replaces one observation vector $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ at a time in $\mathbf{X}$ by sampling it from $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$.
nodes.statement_short: The BRNN's joint distribution is the stationary distribution of Gibbs-style resampling of one $x_t$ at a time from $P_{BRNN}$.

nodes.name: Neural Autoregressive Distribution Estimator (NADE)
nodes.statement: {\bf NADE} The Neural Autoregressive Distribution Estimator (NADE) \citep{uria2014deep} defines a probabilistic model by reconstructing missing components of a vector one at a time in a random order, starting from a fully unobserved vector. Each reconstruction is given by an auto-encoder network that takes as input the observations so far and an auxiliary mask vector that indicates which values are missing.
nodes.statement_short: NADE defines a distribution by reconstructing missing components one at a time in random order, via a masked auto-encoder.

nodes.name: Missingness indicator input
nodes.statement: Firstly, we concatenate an auxiliary binary element to input vectors to indicate a missing input.

nodes.name: NADE joint distribution for time series
nodes.statement: The joint distribution of the time series is defined by first drawing a random permutation $o_d$ of time indices $1\dots T$ and then setting data points observed one by one in that order, starting from a fully missing sequence: \begin{align} P_{\mathrm{NADE}}(\mathbf{X}\mid o_d) = \prod_{d=1}^T P(\mathbf{x}_{o_d} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_{o_{e}}\}_{e=1}^{d-1}). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Draw a random order $o_d$ of time indices and multiply the BRNN conditionals of each point given those already revealed.

nodes.name: NADE ordered factorization
nodes.statement: P_{\mathrm{NADE}}(\mathbf{X}\mid o_d) = \prod_{d=1}^T P(\mathbf{x}_{o_d} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_{o_{e}}\}_{e=1}^{d-1}).

nodes.name: Filling in gaps in binary time series
nodes.statement: The task we aim to solve is to fill in gaps of multiple consecutive data points in high-dimensional binary time series data.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: Why gap inference is non-trivial
nodes.statement: The inference is not trivial for two reasons: firstly, we reconstruct multiple consecutive data points, which are likely to depend on each other, and secondly, we fill in data in the middle of a time series and hence need to consider the data both before and after the gap.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: GSN gap filling
nodes.statement: For filling in gaps with the GSN approach, we first train a bidirectional RNN to estimate $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$. In order to achieve that, we use the structure presented in Section~\ref{sec:bidirectional}. At test time, the gap is first initialized to random values, after which the missing values are sampled from the distribution $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$ one by one in a random order repeatedly to approximate the stationary distribution.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
input: a bidirectional RNN to estimate $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$
nodes.statement_short: Train a BRNN for $P(x_t\mid x_{\neq t})$, initialize the gap randomly, then Gibbs-sample gap points in random order repeatedly.

nodes.name: Train BRNN conditional
nodes.statement: For filling in gaps with the GSN approach, we first train a bidirectional RNN to estimate $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$. In order to achieve that, we use the structure presented in Section~\ref{sec:bidirectional}.
nodes.statement_short: Train the proposed BRNN to output $P_{BRNN}(x_t\mid x_{\neq t})$.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: Random gap initialization
nodes.statement: At test time, the gap is first initialized to random values,
nodes.statement_short: Initialize the gap randomly.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: Gibbs resampling of the gap
nodes.statement: after which the missing values are sampled from the distribution $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$ one by one in a random order repeatedly to approximate the stationary distribution.
nodes.statement_short: Resample gap points one by one in random order, repeatedly.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: Complexity of GSN gap filling
nodes.statement: For the RNN structures used in this paper, the computational complexity of this approach at test time is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)(T+gM))$ where $d$ is the dimensionality of a data point, $c$ is the number of hidden units in the RNN, $T$ is the number of time steps in the data, $g$ is the length of the gap and $M$ is the number of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) steps used for inference.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
assumptions: For the RNN structures used in this paper
conclusions: the computational complexity of this approach at test time is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)(T+gM))$
nodes.statement_short: GSN gap filling costs $O((dc+c^2)(T+gM))$.

nodes.name: NADE gap filling
nodes.statement: For filling in gaps with the NADE approach, we first train a bidirectional RNN where some of the inputs are set to a separate missing value token. At test time, all data points in the gap are first initialized with this token, after which each missing data point is reconstructed once until the whole gap is filled.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
nodes.statement_short: Train a BRNN with a missing-value token; mark the gap missing, then reconstruct each gap point once until filled.

nodes.name: Train BRNN with missing token
nodes.statement: For filling in gaps with the NADE approach, we first train a bidirectional RNN where some of the inputs are set to a separate missing value token.
nodes.statement_short: Train a BRNN with some inputs replaced by the missing token.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: Initialize gap with missing token
nodes.statement: At test time, all data points in the gap are first initialized with this token,
nodes.statement_short: Mark all gap points as missing.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: Sequential one-shot reconstruction
nodes.statement: after which each missing data point is reconstructed once until the whole gap is filled.
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct each missing point once.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: NADE versus GSN computation
nodes.statement: Computationally, the main difference to GSN is that we do not have to sample each reconstructed data point multiple times, but the reconstruction is done in as many steps as there are missing data points in the gap.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: Complexity of NADE gap filling
nodes.statement: For the RNN structures used in this paper, the computational complexity of this approach at test time is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)(T+g))$ where $d$ is the dimensionality of a data point, $c$ is the number of hidden units in the RNN, $g$ is the length of the gap and $T$ is the number of time steps in the data.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
assumptions: For the RNN structures used in this paper
conclusions: the computational complexity of this approach at test time is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)(T+g))$
nodes.statement_short: NADE gap filling costs $O((dc+c^2)(T+g))$.

nodes.name: Bayesian MCMC
nodes.statement:
In addition to the two proposed methods, one can use a unidirectional RNN to solve the same task. We call this method \emph{Bayesian MCMC}. Using a unidirectional RNN for the task of filling in gaps is not trivial, as we need to take into account the probabilities of the values after the gap, which the model does not explicitly do. We therefore resort to a similar approach as the GSN approach, where we replace the $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d
eq t})$ with a unidirectional equivalent for the Gibbs sampling. As the unidirectional RNN models conditional probabilities of the form $P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1})$, we can use Bayes' theorem to derive:  egin{align} \hspace{2em}&\hspace{-2em} P_{\mathrm{RNN}}\left( \mathbf{x}_{t} = \mathbf{a} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_{d}\}_{d
eq t} ight) \ & \propto P_{\mathrm{RNN}} \left( \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{a} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1} ight) P_{\mathrm{RNN}} \left(\{\mathbf{x}_e\}_{e=t+1}^{T} \mid \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{a}, \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1} ight) \ &= \prod_{	au=t}^T P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{	au} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{	au-1}) \Bigr|_{\mathbf{x}_t=\mathbf{a}} \end{align} where $P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{	au} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{	au-1})$ is directly the output of the unidirectional RNN given an input sequence $\mathbf{X}$, where one time step $t$, i.e. the one we Gibbs sample, is replaced by a proposal $\mathbf{a}$. The problem is that we have to go through all possible proposals $\mathbf{a}$ separately to evaluate the probability $P\left( \mathbf{x}_{t} = \mathbf{a} | \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d
eq t} ight)$. We therefore have to evaluate the product of the outputs of the unidirectional RNN for time steps $t \ldots T$ for each possible $\mathbf{a}$.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
nodes.statement_short: Gibbs-sample the gap as in GSN, but compute each conditional from a unidirectional RNN via Bayes' rule, scoring every proposal $a$ over time steps $t..T$.

nodes.name: GSN-style Gibbs sampling with unidirectional conditional
nodes.statement: We therefore resort to a similar approach as the GSN approach, where we replace the $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$ with a unidirectional equivalent for the Gibbs sampling.
nodes.statement_short: Run GSN-style Gibbs sampling with a unidirectional-RNN conditional.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: Evaluate all proposals
nodes.statement: The problem is that we have to go through all possible proposals $\mathbf{a}$ separately to evaluate the probability $P\left( \mathbf{x}_{t} = \mathbf{a} | \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t} \right)$. We therefore have to evaluate the product of the outputs of the unidirectional RNN for time steps $t \ldots T$ for each possible $\mathbf{a}$.
nodes.statement_short: For each proposal $a$, evaluate the RNN output product over $t..T$.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: Bayes conditional of a unidirectional RNN
nodes.statement: As the unidirectional RNN models conditional probabilities of the form $P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1})$, we can use Bayes' theorem to derive: \begin{align} \hspace{2em}&\hspace{-2em} P_{\mathrm{RNN}}\left( \mathbf{x}_{t} = \mathbf{a} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_{d}\}_{d\neq t} \right) \\ & \propto P_{\mathrm{RNN}} \left( \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{a} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1} \right) P_{\mathrm{RNN}} \left(\{\mathbf{x}_e\}_{e=t+1}^{T} \mid \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{a}, \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1} \right) \\ &= \prod_{\tau=t}^T P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{\tau-1}) \Bigr|_{\mathbf{x}_t=\mathbf{a}} \end{align} where $P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{\tau-1})$ is directly the output of the unidirectional RNN given an input sequence $\mathbf{X}$, where one time step $t$, i.e. the one we Gibbs sample, is replaced by a proposal $\mathbf{a}$.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
assumptions: As the unidirectional RNN models conditional probabilities of the form $P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1})$
nodes.statement_short: Via Bayes' theorem, $P(x_t=a\mid x_{\neq t})$ is proportional to the product of RNN predictions from $t$ to $T$ with $x_t=a$.

nodes.name: Bayesian conditional from a unidirectional RNN
nodes.statement: \hspace{2em}&\hspace{-2em} P_{\mathrm{RNN}}\left( \mathbf{x}_{t} = \mathbf{a} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_{d}\}_{d\neq t} \right) \\ & \propto P_{\mathrm{RNN}} \left( \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{a} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1} \right) P_{\mathrm{RNN}} \left(\{\mathbf{x}_e\}_{e=t+1}^{T} \mid \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{a}, \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1} \right) \\ &= \prod_{\tau=t}^T P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{\tau-1}) \Bigr|_{\mathbf{x}_t=\mathbf{a}}
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
nodes.label: eq:onewayrnn

nodes.name: Feasibility of Bayesian MCMC
nodes.statement: In some cases this is feasible to evaluate. For categorical data, e.g. text, there are as many possible values for $\mathbf{a}$ as there are dimensions\footnote{For character-based text, the number of dimensions is the number of characters in the model alphabet.}. However, for other binary data the number of possibilities grows exponentially, and is clearly not feasible to evaluate.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: Complexity of Bayesian MCMC
nodes.statement: For the RNN structures used in this paper, the computational complexity of this approach at test time is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)(T+aTM))$ where $a$ is the number of different values a data point can have, $d$ is the dimensionality of a data point, $c$ is the number of hidden units in the RNN, $T$ is the number of time steps in the data, and $M$ is the number of MCMC steps used for inference.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
assumptions: For the RNN structures used in this paper
conclusions: the computational complexity of this approach at test time is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)(T+aTM))$
nodes.statement_short: Bayesian MCMC costs $O((dc+c^2)(T+aTM))$, with $a$ the number of values a point can take.

nodes.name: The coefficient a separates Bayesian MCMC from GSN
nodes.statement: The critical difference in complexity to the GSN approach is the coefficient $a$, that for categorical data takes the value $d$, for binary vectors $2^d$ and for continuous data is infinite.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: One-gram model
nodes.statement: As a simple baseline model, we also evaluate the \emph{one-gram} log-likelihood of the gaps. The one-gram model assumes a constant context-independent categorical distribution for the categorical task, or a vector of factorial binomial probabilities for the structured prediction task: \begin{equation*} P_{\mathrm{one-gram}}\left(\mathbf{y}_t \right) = \mathrm{f} \left( \mathbf{b}_y \right). \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
nodes.statement_short: Baseline with a constant, context-independent categorical or factorial-Bernoulli output distribution.

nodes.name: Complexity of one-gram baseline
nodes.statement: This can be done in $\mathcal{O}(dg)$.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: One-way inference
nodes.statement: We also compare to \emph{one-way inference}, where the data points in the gap are reconstructed in order without taking the future context into account, using Equations (\ref{eq:uni_y}) and (\ref{eq:uni_h}) directly.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct gap points in order using only past context with the unidirectional RNN equations.

nodes.name: Complexity of one-way inference
nodes.statement: The computational complexity is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)T)$.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: NADE masked training
nodes.statement: For the BRNN used in the NADE method, we add one dimension to the one-hot input which corresponds to a missing value token. During training, in each minibatch we mark $g=5$ consecutive characters every 25 time steps as a gap. During training, the error is propagated only from these gaps. For each gap, we uniformly draw a value from 1 to 5, and set that many characters in the gap to the missing value token.
nodes.section: 5.1 Training details for categorical prediction task
nodes.statement_short: Add a missing-token input; in each minibatch mark length-5 gaps every 25 steps, mask a random number of their characters, and backpropagate only from gaps.

nodes.name: Add missing-value input dimension
nodes.statement: For the BRNN used in the NADE method, we add one dimension to the one-hot input which corresponds to a missing value token.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the one-hot input with a missing-token dimension.

nodes.name: Mark gaps
nodes.statement: During training, in each minibatch we mark $g=5$ consecutive characters every 25 time steps as a gap.
nodes.statement_short: Mark 5-character gaps every 25 steps.

nodes.name: NADE masked and NADE no mask
nodes.statement: For comparison, we also train a similar network, but without masking. In that variant, the error is therefore propagated from all time steps. We refer to ``NADE'' masked and ``NADE no mask'', respectively, for these two training methods.

nodes.name: Weight initialization
nodes.statement: For all the models, the weight elements are drawn from the uniform distribution: $w_{i,j}\sim \mathcal{U}\left[-s, s\right]$ where $s=1$ for the input to hidden layer, and following \citet{glorot2010understanding}, where $s=\sqrt{6/\left(d_{in} + d_{out}\right)}$ for the hidden-to-hidden and the hidden-to output layers. The biases are initialized to zero.
nodes.section: 5.1 Training details for categorical prediction task
nodes.statement_short: Uniform weight initialization (scale 1 for input weights, Glorot scale elsewhere) and zero biases.

nodes.name: SGD training with gradient normalization
nodes.statement: The networks are trained using stochastic gradient descent and the gradient is calculated using backpropagation through time. We use a minibatch size of 40, i.e. each minibatch consists of 40 randomly sampled sequences of length 250. As the gradients tend to occasionally ``blow up'' when training RNNs \citep{bengio1994learning,pascanu2013difficulty}, we normalize the gradients at each update to have length one. The step size is set to 0.25 for all layers in the beginning of training, and it is linearly decayed to zero during training.

nodes.statement_short: Minibatch SGD with BPTT, gradients normalized to unit length, step size 0.25 linearly decayed to zero.

nodes.name: Gap log-likelihood evaluation measure
nodes.statement: At test time, we evaluate the models by calculating the mean log-likelihood of the correct value of gaps of five consecutive missing values in test data.
nodes.definiendum: mean log-likelihood of the correct value of gaps

nodes.name: GSN and Bayesian MCMC gap evaluation
nodes.statement: In the GSN and Bayesian MCMC approaches, we first set the five values in the gap to a random value for the categorical prediction task, or to zero for the structured prediction task. We then sample all five values in the gap in random order, and repeat the procedure for $M=100$ MCMC steps\footnote{$M=100$ MCMC steps means that each value in the gap of $g=5$ will be resampled $M/g=20$ times}. For evaluating the log-likelihood of the correct value for the string, we force the last five steps to sample the correct value, and store the probability of the model sampling those values. We also evaluate the probability of reconstructing correctly the individual data points by not forcing the last five time steps to sample the correct value, but by storing the probability of reconstructing the correct value for each data point separately. We run the MCMC chain 100 times and use the log of the mean of the likelihoods of predicting the correct value over these 100 runs.
nodes.statement_short: Initialize the gap, run $M=100$ Gibbs sweeps, force the last five samples to the truth to score the gap, and average likelihoods over 100 chains.

nodes.name: Gap initialization
nodes.statement: In the GSN and Bayesian MCMC approaches, we first set the five values in the gap to a random value for the categorical prediction task, or to zero for the structured prediction task.
nodes.statement_short: Random (text) or zero (music) gap initialization.

nodes.name: MCMC sweeps
nodes.statement: then sample all five values in the gap in random order, and repeat the procedure for $M=100$ MCMC steps\footnote{$M=100$ MCMC steps means that each value in the gap of $g=5$ will be resampled $M/g=20$ times}.
nodes.statement_short: Resample the gap values in random order for $M=100$ steps.

nodes.name: Forced final sampling
nodes.statement: For evaluating the log-likelihood of the correct value for the string, we force the last five steps to sample the correct value, and store the probability of the model sampling those values.
nodes.statement_short: Force the last five samples to the truth and store their probability.

nodes.name: Per-point reconstruction probability
nodes.statement: We also evaluate the probability of reconstructing correctly the individual data points by not forcing the last five time steps to sample the correct value, but by storing the probability of reconstructing the correct value for each data point separately.
nodes.statement_short: Store each point's probability of correct reconstruction without forcing.

nodes.name: Average over 100 chains
nodes.statement: We run the MCMC chain 100 times and use the log of the mean of the likelihoods of predicting the correct value over these 100 runs.
nodes.statement_short: Log of the mean likelihood over 100 chains.

nodes.name: One-way inference evaluation
nodes.statement: When evaluating the performance of one-directional inference, we use a similar approach to MCMC. However, when evaluating the log-likelihood of the entire gap, we only construct it once in sequential order, and record the probabilities of reconstructing the correct value. When evaluating the probability of reconstructing the correct value for each data point separately, we use the same approach as for MCMC and sample the gap 100 times, recording for each step the probability of sampling the correct value. The result for each data point is the log of the mean of the likelihoods over these 100 runs.
nodes.statement_short: Score the whole gap by one sequential reconstruction; score individual points by 100 sampled reconstructions.

nodes.name: Reuse MCMC evaluation scheme
nodes.statement: When evaluating the performance of one-directional inference, we use a similar approach to MCMC.
nodes.statement_short: Follow the MCMC evaluation scheme.

nodes.name: Single sequential gap reconstruction
nodes.statement: However, when evaluating the log-likelihood of the entire gap, we only construct it once in sequential order, and record the probabilities of reconstructing the correct value.
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct the gap once in order and record correct-value probabilities.

nodes.name: Repeated per-point sampling
nodes.statement: When evaluating the probability of reconstructing the correct value for each data point separately, we use the same approach as for MCMC and sample the gap 100 times, recording for each step the probability of sampling the correct value.
nodes.statement_short: Sample the gap 100 times recording per-step correct probabilities.

nodes.name: Per-point log-mean likelihood
nodes.statement: The result for each data point is the log of the mean of the likelihoods over these 100 runs.
nodes.statement_short: Per-point score is the log mean likelihood.

nodes.name: Exact NADE gap evaluation
nodes.statement: For NADE, we set the five time steps in the gap to the missing value token. We then reconstruct them one by one to the correct value, and record the probability of the correct reconstruction. We repeat this process for all possible permutations of the order in which to do the reconstruction, and therefore acquire the exact probability of the correct reconstruction given the model and the data. We also evaluate the individual character reconstruction probabilities by recording the probability of sampling the correct value given all other values in the gap are set to missing.
nodes.statement_short: Mask the gap, reconstruct it to the truth in every order of the five points to get the exact gap probability.

nodes.name: Mask the gap
nodes.statement: For NADE, we set the five time steps in the gap to the missing value token.
nodes.statement_short: Set the gap to the missing token.

nodes.name: Sequential correct reconstruction
nodes.statement: We then reconstruct them one by one to the correct value, and record the probability of the correct reconstruction.
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct to the true values, recording probabilities.

nodes.name: All reconstruction orders
nodes.statement: We repeat this process for all possible permutations of the order in which to do the reconstruction, and therefore acquire the exact probability of the correct reconstruction given the model and the data.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat for all orders to get the exact probability.

nodes.name: Individual reconstruction probabilities
nodes.statement: We also evaluate the individual character reconstruction probabilities by recording the probability of sampling the correct value given all other values in the gap are set to missing.
nodes.statement_short: Per-point probability with the rest of the gap missing.

nodes.name: Bayesian MCMC best; GSN and NADE beat one-way inference
nodes.statement: From Table~\ref{tab:bps} we can see that the Bayesian MCMC method seems to yield the best results, while GSN or NADE outperform one-way inference.
conclusions: the Bayesian MCMC method seems to yield the best results
GSN or NADE outperform one-way inference

nodes.name: One-way inference strong on Piano and JSB
nodes.statement: It is worth noting that in the most difficult data sets, piano and JSB, oneway inference performs very well.
assumptions: in the most difficult data sets, piano and JSB

nodes.name: GSN mixing behaviour
nodes.statement: The figure indicates that the music data sets mix fairly well, as the performance of GSN quickly saturates. However, for the Wikipedia data, the performance could probably be even further improved by letting the MCMC chain run for more than $M=100$ steps.
conclusions: the music data sets mix fairly well
for the Wikipedia data, the performance could probably be even further improved by letting the MCMC chain run for more than $M=100$ steps

nodes.name: Gap edges are easier to predict
nodes.statement: As expected, all methods except for one-way inference are better at predicting characters close to both edges of the gap.
conclusions: all methods except for one-way inference are better at predicting characters close to both edges of the gap

nodes.name: BRNNs outperform published unidirectional RNNs at gap size one
nodes.statement: In Table~\ref{tab:nll_train} (supplementary material) we can see that the BRNNs expectedly outperform previously published results with unidirectional RNNs, which indicates that the models have been trained successfully.
conclusions: the BRNNs expectedly outperform previously published results with unidirectional RNNs

nodes.name: Effect of the training missingness pattern
nodes.statement: It would be interesting to study the effect of the missingness pattern used in training, on the learned representations and predictions.

nodes.name: Reconstruction-only NADE training hurts single-value NLL
nodes.statement: We can see from Table~\ref{tab:nll_train} that the model we trained for NADE where we only used the reconstructions as the training signal has a worse performance than the BRNN for reconstructing single values. This indicates that these differences in training have a significant impact on the quality of the final trained probabilistic model.
conclusions: the model we trained for NADE where we only used the reconstructions as the training signal has a worse performance than the BRNN for reconstructing single values

nodes.name: RNN vs BRNN at optimal hidden-layer size
nodes.statement: It remains an open question which approach would work best given an optimal size of the hidden layers.

nodes.name: Multiplicative missingness gating
nodes.statement: Specifically to our NADE approach, it might make sense to replace the regular additive connection from the missingness indicator input to the hidden activations in Eq.~(\ref{eq:bi_hf},\ref{eq:bi_hb}), by a multiplicative connection that somehow gates the dynamics mappings $\mathbf{W}_h^f$ and $\mathbf{W}_h^b$.

nodes.name: Independent Bernoulli output limitation
nodes.statement: The midi music data is an example of a structured prediction task: Components of the output vector depend strongly on each other. However, our model assumes independent Bernoulli distributions for them.
